content: Bronchitis is characterized by inflammation of the bronchi, which are the medium and large-sized airways in the respiratory system. Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting condition typically caused by viral or bacterial infections. In contrast, chronic bronchitis is a distinct clinical entity and is classified as part of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Chronic bronchitis is defined by the presence of a productive cough lasting for at least three months in two consecutive years. The inflammatory response in bronchitis involves the bronchial epithelium reacting to infections or irritants, leading to thickening of the mucosa in the bronchi and trachea. In chronic bronchitis, hallmark pathological features include hyperplasia and hypertrophy of goblet cells in the airway, which result in excessive mucus production and contribute to airway obstruction. Microscopically, the airway walls show infiltration by inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils. This inflammation is followed by scarring and remodeling, which thicken the airway walls and narrow the small airways. As the disease progresses, metaplasia and fibrosis of the lower airways may occur, further limiting airflow. Acute bronchitis is more commonly observed in young children and older adults, while chronic bronchitis is prevalent among geriatric patients. Chronic bronchitis is more frequently diagnosed in Caucasian individuals compared to other racial groups, but it affects males and females equally. Risk factors for acute bronchitis include age, seasonal variations, and immunization status. The most significant risk factor for developing chronic bronchitis is cigarette smoking. Additional risk factors include exposure to occupational pollutants (e.g., cadmium, silica), air pollution, and genetic predispositions such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting lower respiratory tract infection that typically presents with a cough lasting up to three weeks. Chronic bronchitis, on the other hand, tends to worsen gradually over time and can ultimately lead to death. The rate of disease progression varies among individuals and is influenced by the degree of airflow obstruction. Early recognition of chronic bronchitis and smoking cessation are critical for improving prognosis. Smoking cessation, proper hand hygiene, vaccination, and minimizing occupational exposures are essential strategies to reduce the severity and risk of bronchitis. Bronchitis is classified into two major categories based on the chronicity of symptoms: acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis.
